utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina, Cermak, and Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness 136, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave during closed session. You'll testify with the protective measures as granted, that is, face distortion and pseudonym, and the reasons for the decision will follow in a public written decision. Whether it will be public in every respect is still to be seen, but that is for the public to know what the reasons are. Mr. Waespi, are you ready to examine Witness 136?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As you know, we filed a motion to have two witness statements admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I would like to show these statements to the witness, but before I do that I would like to show her her personal details that should be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet. Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if it could be shown to Your Honours and the members of the Defence first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For all practical purposes the Chamber considers it's enough if at least one member of each team has seen it so that we do not have all the case managers to verify whether they have more important work to do. Could an exhibit number be assigned to it. May I take it that it will be P1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be Exhibit P1 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, can you please confirm that these are your personal details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it there are no objections. Therefore, P1 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If 65 ter number 04763 could be brought up and please do not broadcast this piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember having given a witness statement in July 1996 to members of the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the Chamber usually is not informed -- well, we could try to find out. Are we talking about which of the two statements at this moment? Is it the 1996 statement or is it the other statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's the first one 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the first one, the 1996 statement. Madam Registrar, that would be marked for identification number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you remember having been visited by investigators of the ICTY and having given a statement in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, and this is indeed my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review this statement before you came today to the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was shown this statement right after it was taken, and I signed every page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again you were asked back in 1996, would your answers be the same as recorded in this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same, but I would probably be able to provide more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it could be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One additional question. When you said you signed that statement, I take it that you did so because it accurately reflected the content of your statement. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against admission? No. P2 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have added under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. In that respect, Mr. President, we'll try to perhaps have a redacted statement. It's easier for everybody to quote it later in closing submissions if it's not under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the time being, the complete and unredacted version is admitted under seal. It could be replaced at a later stage by two, that is one complete version and one redacted version. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you give a second statement on the 11th of June, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while the witness is answering, could we please bring up 65 ter number 4760.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, not to be shown to the public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did give a statement in June 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And is that because it accurately reflected what your testimony would be at that time or today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely because it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you look at the screen right now. Is that this second statement you gave in June 2007?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, again if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again unless the parties would have understood this otherwise, your question, Mr. Waespi, you asked whether this accurately reflected what your testimony would be at the time or today. I take it that you wanted to ask the witness whether it reflected accurately the content of her statement at that time and whether she would give the same answers if these questions were put to her today again. That's what you want to ask the witness, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is what you confirmed, Witness 136?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. I would make the same statement, but perhaps with some more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not see any party rising for objections. Therefore, P3 is admitted under seal for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the next potential exhibit 65 ter number 04769 could be put onto the screen and this can be made public, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, while that's being done, in your witness statement, in your first one which is now Exhibit 2, in the last paragraph on page 2 you say that on the 4th of August, 1995, you left your apartment and ran through the town to the south barracks in Knin. I would like you to look at this image once it comes up and identify the building where you were staying at that time. Don't give the address. Just tell us where your building was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, this 65 ter number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal, I take it, Mr. Waespi. If it identifies the place where the witness was living at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it's a larger building, residential building, so I don't think the location would identify this witness. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- the lower part of this an image could be enhanced. Lower right part, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Looking at this image now, Witness, do you see the building you were staying at on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: With the help of Mr. Usher, can you please take a pen and mark approximately the building you were staying at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just look at it carefully, then once you decide where it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, can you tell us or show us, rather, the route you took when you went to the UN compound on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I was accompanied by a Portuguese man from the UN and another female interpreter. We ran next to the kindergarten, the infirmary. We stopped for a while here in the shelter in this building, but because the Portuguese man was with us he didn't feel all that comfortable with the other people there, and so we went out into the main road again past the department store. Could you perhaps -- okay. The main road, and this is where we were picked up by the UN APCs, and we continued on to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please mark with an A, letter A, next to it where you were picked up by the UN APCs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't be very specific. It's right in the middle of the street here. I know that we passed this house here, and I fainted in front of the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And let's be -- and just a reminder to everybody that the size of the image shouldn't be changed now because if that's being done we lose it. So you have to continue on this image, Witness. Can you continue beyond the letter A the route, as far as you recall, you took to reach the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And lastly, if you could indicate with a letter B where you said that there was a shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as I left the building the house next to the apartment building was completely destroyed, and I wondered at the time whether anyone could have survived there. Should I put a B there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Can you make -- it looks like a D to me but maybe it's a B. I just note it's the mark --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just add again a B lower to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. That building was completely destroyed but what kind of building was that, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a residential building, a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, now, how long did you stay in the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until the 16th of September. Some 45 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did you do during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first three days, because I'm not from Knin, I interpreted at the gate. I would welcome the people who would come to the gate. I took care of them in the compound, and later on I started going on patrols from the 11th of August onwards in Knin and in the village around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who were the people you welcomed to the gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People who came to the gate were Serbs and Croats. I remember some Croats. I know their names. They came in from the area of Cetina which was the area that I covered in my work as an interpreter. Those were mostly children, women, the elderly, pregnant women. I saw some people with mental disabilities, people in wheelchairs, or people from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If this aerial imagery could be saved and entered into the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- the aerial photograph marked for identification as P4 is now tendered with the markings of the witness on it. Any objection? No objection. P4 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a few remaining questions for the witness, but could at this time already 65 ter number 04768 be brought up. This is that large map, so it may take some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you went on patrols from the 11th of August onwards in Knin and in the village around it. I take it you said villages around it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, villages and hamlets around Knin and further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to admit when I was offered to leave the first time I refused, but in the end, on the 9th of August, I agreed to go out to attend a meeting at the police station. Then I changed my mind again because I was scared, and I said I refused to go out. But then I realised that if I didn't go out that soon they would engage interpreters from Zagreb, Sibenik, Zadar and that nobody would ever learn what had happened to my grandmother, to my relatives, to my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you say "they would engage interpreters," who -- whom were you accompanying on these patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was one of the few who agreed to leave the compound, so I accompanied the UN civilian police, the UN military observers, the press office. All of the foreigners, the human rights office, all of those who at various points left the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, from what I've heard until now, approximately 80 per cent is perfectly clear from the 92 ter statement. Of course I do not know how you want to use your 30 minutes. You said you need them for clarification and adding anything. If we would continue this way, I fear for the time it will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's basically it. A couple more questions. It's also to -- to be honest, to be give the witness a chance to address in a few minutes what she has seen before the Defence will have a chance to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, in front of you you can see a map displayed. Do you know what this map is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Knin area, and it also shows the area further afield. The places that are marked are places that I visited after Operation Storm. I had been allowed by General Cermak to move about Knin itself, but I dodged this limitation, and at my own risk I ventured further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So just to clarify, the places, the villages that have been marked in pink, these are the places you have visited on patrol in and around Knin in August 1995 when you were an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these villages are the villages you describe in these two witness statements we have just admitted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be admitted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be Exhibit P5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P5, and that is -- Mr. Waespi, would it be a good idea that we would have this same map in evidence but then without the explanations and the examples, the green and the red spots, so that we have a kind of a virgin map just showing because otherwise other witnesses who would have to explain on the basis of the map where they went might be influenced by the markings on this map. So this P5 is including information about scheduled killings and examples of destruction and if you would, at a suitable moment, tender a clean map so we can work with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certain, Mr. President. If the next potential exhibit 65 ter number 04766 could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you look at the screen in front of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi. This should not be shown to the public, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's safer not to show it to the public, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Only since the name appears. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, can you -- do you recognise this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours what it is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are persons who were killed and buried at the Knin cemetery. I assume since I can see the names of persons of this list who were killed in Grubori and Boraci from the village of Bosic that the list was compiled sometime later in August. I took stock of all the lines of graves and the names of people there who were buried there. A total of 17 in the first row, five unidentified. In the second row a total of 45, 35 unidentified, and so on and so forth. I do have to say one thing these figures that I can see on the margin are slightly confusing. I tried to add up and see how many people had been killed. I know there were another two locations at the Knin cemetery, therefore, I assume that a page is missing that should accompany this list. So that's as to the calculations here on the margin of this page. I can't say what that's in reference to. I suppose I was trying to add up the separate figures for these three different locations within the Knin cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I see that in between the names there are a few NNs. Can you explain what these NNs mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I put the list together by walking from grave to grave, from cross to cross, in a manner of speaking, and I tried to observe how many unidentified bodies were buried between the individual graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this list could be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that list would receive number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be Exhibit P6 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6. Any objection? No objection. P6 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last exhibit I would like to discuss with you, Witness, is another list. This is 65 ter number 4767.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, can it be shown to the public or can it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It can be shown to the public, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while that's being done, when did you go to see the cemetery in Knin, the time, the occasion you wrote down these names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the cemetery several times. Once because there was lady whose husband had been killed and she was on her way to the cemetery accompanied by a security official. However, she couldn't locate the grave, so I went with her to give her a hand. I found it in a different place within the Knin cemetery. There was this other time that I went with one from the press office, an official. However, we were turned away because there was a burial underway. Although we were at a distance of no more than a hundred metres, one could still sense the stench of decomposing bodies. I did go another two or three times. I can't say exactly. Once I was there with my station commander who was a -- a Russian and the deputy chief of sector of the UN, the chief of the Sector South civilian police who was a Dane.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Now, looking at the screen in front of you, do you recognise this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the list that we're looking at is the first list that the Croatian police provided to the UN members.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you present when the UN members were provided with this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received several lists. I think a total of three of four, perhaps more. I wasn't there every time the list was handed to us. I can't remember if I was actually physically present when this one was handed to us; however, as soon as the list reached the UN base, I was allowed to make copies of it and to circulate these copies to people who were in the compound, just so they could check whether any of their relatives or acquaintances were on that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would turn into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us you received the list from the Croatian authorities. Do you recall who it was from the Croatian authorities who gave the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say exactly now whether it was in the station commander's office, the Knin station commander's office, or Cedo Romanic or Zvonko Gambiroza, but I'm 100 per cent certain about one thing. The list originated from the Croatian police and I have to say I was quite surprised at the time that we were now receiving a list of those killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the list could be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objections? In the absence of objections, P6 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, was it P7 or P6?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I made a mistake. It's P -- it's P7. It had not been yet marked for identification, but that is the last document. The 65 ter number was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 4767, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4767 is P7 admitted into evidence. Please proceed. Under seal again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes the questions I have for the witness. I didn't intend to show her the situation reports from CIVPOL she was involved in because we had moved to move them into evidence -- witness statements, because all these exhibits were discussed in her witness statement. There is a reference in each of the witness statements as to her memory that these were authentic documents. And I can tell Your Honours which of these exhibits we invite you to -- to tender, and I think there might be one or two objections from the Gotovina Defence after we met with them yesterday, and I'm happy to address the relevancy of these exhibits. The first one would be Exhibit 65 ter number, and I now go through the list we provided to Your Honours and Defence, the Exhibit number is -- the 65 ter number is 1039.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to be sure, do I understand that these exhibits are not directly attached to the witness statement, although especially the 2007 statement refers to quite a lot of these exhibits and you tender them separately as exhibits so they need a number to be marked for identification individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think they do need a number and they are all referenced, as you rightly pointed out, in the 2007 statement and some of them in addition in the 1996 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, 65 ter number 1039 would receive --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would be Exhibit P8 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P8 marked for identification. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The objection I had with regard to that, and I will say that we sat down to discuss this at some length, it's a situation report, obviously not signed by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That talks about two individuals that are wives of -- excuse me, the husbands of two women that came into the area. Now, I say this, Judge, that we have well over 200 killings with the scheduled killings and the clarification of indictment killings, and the names that we have before us here in this sitrep are on none of those lists. So while we have some -- well over 250 murders, the two that are in the sitrep are not in that list, and there's no tying up of this as to what happened to these people or anything else. They're not on these lists that have been presented by the Prosecution so far, so the issue is one of simply relevancy. The way it's coming out is that these people were killed, or that's what the Prosecution, I believe, would like the Chamber to believe, yet there has been no closing of the loop that these people are actually dead or what circumstances they died under.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's correct what Mr. Kehoe said, that although there is information that these two victims were killed, but they are not on our list of killed persons, but if you look at the indictment at paragraph 33, last two sentences, this -- the Prosecution theory is not just the killings. It's the persecutions, it's the harassment of the civilian population. It's the inhumane treatment, count 9. So that's a perfectly good example to show what the UN agencies, to whom the witness was an interpreter, found that was part of the strategy to expel the Serbs from the region. So it's less the killings than the disappearance of these two soldiers who were clearly hors de combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respond to that, Judge. These individuals are hors de combat. And I am concerned, Mr. President, that just laying these names out, as if there is some idea that they've been killed without any follow-up information, is prejudicial to the Defence and there's simply no way to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will decide the matter. At this moment P8 remains marked for identification. We'll consider the matter, and we'll give a decision on it, if possible, immediately after the break so that you know where you are in your cross-examination of the witness. Yes. Next one, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 1793 65 ter would be -- I didn't hear you. Use my microphone. That would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P10 marked for identification. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Similar to the objection before. There's been no follow-up information concerning this woman. This seems to be an incident that took place in the course of some type of combat operations and this woman was caught in the crossfire. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Again that's the same argument the Prosecution has. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand, therefore, that the suggestion that was put by Mr. Kehoe that you would by this evidence want to prove murder is not what your intention is?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we just have the first witness and a few pieces -- eight pieces of evidence. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore it's not that you deduce from this document alone who was the suspected perpetrator of what happened to this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not at this time. Not beyond what's contained in the document. If in the document it says "Croatian soldiers" or "Croatian military" which it sometimes does, then that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That clarifies the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further comments? If not, P10. The Chamber will consider and decide on the admission of P10. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC

utterances.text: Thank you. P9, Mr. Waespi, you had stated it would only be page 1 of P9; correct?

utterances.text: I just wanted to make that clear, Your Honour. I don't think that was clear before, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P9 is only the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems on the basis of the full name, at least to the extent that I understand these codes, it goes from 2407 to 2409, which suggests three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We have discussed that with the Defence and we agreed that only the first page would be relevant for this witness. There will be other witnesses who hopefully will introduce the whole range but for this specific witness, only the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then take it that P9 consists only of 0035-2407 and nothing more?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Please proceed. And then admission of course is accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt but now that we're discussing P9, I really can't understand how this document is relevant since the wording of the document itself tells us that there is suspicion, no more than that, that two persons were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, P9 was tendered. I gave an opportunity to object. You didn't use that opportunity. It's now admitted into evidence. The only the thing we're discussing now is whether it's a three- or one-page document. May I -- please stand up whenever there's any -- when there's any objection. utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Your understanding is entirely correct. I just wanted to draw your attention to this portion of the document. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's an incident report. Madam Registrar, that would be, may I take it, P11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't see Mr. Mikulicic. No objection against P11? Then P11 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi. If you're consulting each other if you switch off the microphone that at least avoids that the public is following your discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can. What -- as a matter of fact, what I have on my mind is that we finish with these documents before the break. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next document, I believe, is 4124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be P11, I take it, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As soon as I take over, mistakes are made. I apologise. P12 marked for identification. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I apologise. This was, frankly, I believe my last objection and again it falls into the same category of -- we have a situation where Croatian government is encouraging people that gives them -- let's them go back and three unidentified people are coming in, who a soldier -- the Croatian soldiers is described to give this woman a hard time. I know Your Honour did address the hearsay issue, but this is a situation with a woman talking to a translator that then is put in a document that is written by another party about people who are completely unidentified. The attenuation issue here is my objection and I don't think that the Chamber can properly rely on the information on this because of that attenuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Kehoe actually gave the answer. At the time the Croatian government allegedly tells the people, encouraging people to come back. The opposite happens on the ground, that the Croatian soldiers, you know, harass civilians, and that's part of the Prosecution's case. And it's impossible, Your Honours, to identify each of these single soldiers. I believe it's enough to say -- ask the witness or whoever made this report, records, that these are Croatian soldiers in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The difficulty with this, Judge, and I will make this brief, is that every male in that area has camouflage on and how can we address this, frankly, second or third-hand hearsay to determine who these people are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I see the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read in some of the statements that even males were wearing civilian clothes, so the sweeping statement that every male was wearing camouflage, I cannot completely follow that. Your point has been taken the Chamber will consider and decide the matter. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's two more documents. The first one, 3543.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, that would be.

utterances.text: P13. May I take it from the fact that there was an agreement between two of the three parties, and Mr. Kehoe just announced that he expressed his last objection, that P13 finds no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The last one is 1920.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the same what I just said is true and, Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then to cut matters short, P14 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just one last point, Mr. President. Of course you're aware I don't need to remind you of the difference between the admissibility and the weight which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber is aware, yes, of the difference of that. Mr. Waespi, I have not completely checked every single detail, but I remember that in the statement sometimes reference is made not only to interpreters but also to names of interpreters, if sometimes first names. Have you carefully checked all these materials and whether in view of the witness protection there needs to be any redactions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think there need to be redactions. We might even have to go back and admit them under seal because sometimes the first name of the witness is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was referring to. That means that those exhibits admitted at this very moment are admitted under seal out of an abundance of caution, and that you and the Defence will verify whether there's any identifying issue in relation to that document. The Chamber expects a report on this not later than by tomorrow at the beginning of the session. Any further matter at this moment? Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before we break, which I presume is immediately before cross-examination begins, I would -- well, let me say as a background matter we haven't completed the discussions about the lengths of time that would precede the -- excuse me, the lengths of time for disclosure of exhibits before a witness testified for either side, but I think it's fair to say that the -- it was understood that for the disclosure of Defence exhibits they would at least be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The beginning of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should be more precise: After the examination-in-chief had been concluded. Is there a list of exhibits the Defence of any of the accused would wish to use and to be communicated to Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Our case manager Ms. Katalinic advised me that she has just sent an e-mail of what we intend to use. There are two additional demonstrative exhibits in light of the direct examination that we also wish to use and that will be disclosed right now as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then for the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No documents have come to mind yet. Of course it always depends on what happens before me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then for the Markac Defence. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, Your Honour, for the time being we don't have any documents that we intend to use in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the parties are encouraged to continue their discussions on the matter so that we would not have to rely on ad hoc decisions but will have a standard to be set. Witness 136, we'll have a break now. After the break you'll be cross-examined by counsel for the various defendants. Is there an order already established among yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe with this witness, Your Honour, I consulted with my co-counsel and I'll begin first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll begin first, and is there -- I did understand that there should be no time problems as far as this witness is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll first give you decisions on the exhibits P8, P10, and P12. I'll start with the -- with P10. Could we have P10 on the screen for a second. Yes. I asked to have P10 on the screen because P1792 was, as you informed us, remained by 1793 for better legibility. Now, what we had, my hard copy, made it impossible to read the name of the village. Therefore, I thought that it might be that reading the name of the village would be improved by the new version, but I now see that P10 is as badly legible in the translation. Mr. Waespi, is it still the old one that is attached, that you have not yet replaced 1792 by 1793?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It should be replaced. It's either 1793 or 1792, which is the better copy. So it's 1792, which is the clearly legible copy. I have it with me. I can give you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But of course we got the impression that 1793 was the better legible copy, although the transcript might not be for the full 100 per cent transparent in this respect. So it's now 1792 is the better legible copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. If it was my mistake then I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I then take it that we can read the name of the village in that one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It's Ivanici, the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having clarified this, the Chamber admits P10 in the best legible copy into evidence. The Chamber shares the view of the Defence of Mr. Gotovina that the weight that could be given to this moment -- at this moment is very limited, but it's a matter of weight rather than of admissibility, but it's well-understood the point you've made, and even if it's no reason for admissibility it's something the Chamber is clearly aware of. Then we have -- Mr. Waespi, I'm now going to P12. Could we have that on the screen as well. Mr. Waespi, about the legibility of this document, what's your opinion compared to the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I -- when I checked it this morning again, I realised same problem. I made about 15 hard copies of this document if it assists you right now and we can certainly get it scanned in later so we have a better legible copy for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There were no complaints by the parties about it. I don't know. Perhaps they read the translation. I take it this is all the result of marking which not finally makes illegible the text and therefore also not untranslatable, the text --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I could read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would -- yes, if you could read relevant lines then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It reads in the middle after Drpa Dusan house, it goes on: "And beaten him and told him to leave his house. After that, they came to her house and told her that they will kill them and burn the house if they don't leave the house. One of the soldiers beaten Drpa Milica two times by stick and told them they will come to see if they're still there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it it doesn't change the position of the Defence teams? Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. The Chamber admits this document into evidence, invites the Prosecution to replace the version in better legible copy in the e-court system. There is a bit more information here, but of course the weight is still to be considered, because the Chamber well understands the doubts expressed by the Gotovina Defence. Then we'll move to P8. P8 also gives a bit more information but with a similar observation as what weight that could be attached to it. The objections are not such that the Chamber would deny admission into evidence of this document. Therefore, P8, P10, and P12 are admitted into evidence. Witness 136, this seems to be a lot of bookkeeping perhaps for you. You'll now be cross-examined first by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning. I'd like to ask you a couple of questions, some questions not only about what you talked about today but from your witness statements. Now, Witness 136, I would like to take you back to the period of time prior to Operation Storm, and I believe you informed the Office of the Prosecutor that some two months prior to Operation Storm, the UN asked if you wanted to be an evacuation list, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So did that take place as early as May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot claim that with any certainty. Perhaps it was two months before Operation Storm, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the UN also told you that you should have an evacuation bag packed at all times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Since I agreed to be put on the evacuation list, I was automatically given recommendations as to what I should put in my evacuation bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And there were many employees from the Knin town working at the United Nations base that also received that same information, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but you have to bear in mind that I did not have my close family there, and that is why I didn't have any problems putting my name on the list, whereas my colleagues could not put their names on the list and leave their parents, brothers, and sisters behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the information that the United Nations was collecting a list for evacuation was disseminated to the civilian population in Knin, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was communicated to the United Nations personnel, civilian personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the civilian personnel then went and told their families in the town, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, that led to a building up of fear within the civilian population in Knin, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many elements why there was this build-up of fear in Knin. I worked in the Vrlika area, and when all the nine UN stations were shut down, when the Vrlika station was shut down, the very fact that the UN was withdrawing in a way it frightened the people from Vrlika. Cetina had been shelled several times before Operation Storm. People couldn't go out into the field to harvest their crops and that is why so-called harvest teams were set up. I was a member of one such team, and we were supposed to make people relax a little bit and go out and harvest their crops because their livelihood depended on that. Their survival depended on that. So this affected the people there. This is what also made them be afraid. I know that because I worked in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ma'am, so the answer to the question is yes, that by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kehoe. Your question was: "Well, madam, that led to a building up of fear." What that refers to is quite unclear in your question. It was about issuing an invitation to be on a list, further distributing this. Could you please put your question in such a way that there's no ambiguity in any way, especially if a few lines later you tell the witness that the answer to an unclear question where the witness gave a very clear response, that that was a yes to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will ask the question with more clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that the witness identified most of the implicit problems of your question, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, the fact that the United Nations told its employees that they were putting together an evacuation list two months to Operation Storm was, as you told the Prosecution, one more element that built fear with the people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, in my case it did not. The very fact that I stayed there until the very last minute shows that I was perhaps a little naive. The fact is that three days before Operation Storm, a Portuguese man told me that there would be an attack on Knin, but I didn't take it that seriously. And many of my friends did not take that seriously, but what they did take seriously was what had happened in the Vrlika area. I'm giving you this example because I know that for a fact. I was there. Croatian army positions were already visible up above the Cetina fields, and people couldn't go out and harvest their crops, and without harvesting their crops they could not survive. That was one of the key elements that led to this sentiment of fear in the area of Vrlika. So now I'm talking specifically about Vrlika.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ma'am, and then let me ask the question with more clarity, putting you aside. Did that UN evacuation list cause fear in the other employees for the UN besides you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already told you that I myself was not afraid. As far as I know, my colleagues were not afraid either, because if they had been afraid they would have resigned from their jobs in the UN and they would have fled on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall writing an e-mail to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 6th of March, 2008, where you wrote: "I remembered also one more element that was building the fear with the people prior to Operation Storm. Actually, all interpreters were asked maybe one to two months prior to Storm if we would like to be on a UN evacuation list in case something happened."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You did say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to the days prior to Operation Storm. In your witness statement, you noted that people were leaving Knin in buses, full buses, ten days prior to the attack. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, but it was mothers with small children who were leaving. If I had small children at the time I would not have stayed there for a single day, because conditions for small children were awful. There was no electricity, no food. It was impossible to get proper infant food at that time. And electricity, there was no electricity for well-known reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So at least ten days prior to the attack, women and children were being -- were leaving Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were leaving Knin even before that, those who were in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And prior, just prior to Operation Storm, you told the Prosecutor that extra buses were put on -- put to work to take people from Knin to Belgrade. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've told you that some elements of this build-up of fear, such as the shelling, the incidents that occurred at the demarcation lines, the shelling of Cetina, influenced the people from Cetina to withdraw towards Knin, and this created fear among the people of Knin, and it was quite natural for women with small children to try and seek shelter elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But, ma'am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 136, 136, could I invite you to carefully listen to the question that was put to you. The question was whether you told the Prosecutor that extra buses were put to work to take people from Knin to Belgrade. Quite a simple question, whether there were extra buses from Knin to Belgrade, yes or no, and whether you told this to the Prosecution. Could you please respond to that question. Mr. Waespi, I imagine what you're about to say, but could we first hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, and I do apologise for not responding to that question. It is true, but you have to take into account the fact that some people who had private businesses exploited the fear of the people, and they put on those additional buses to work in order to earn money off those frightened women who wanted to leave to Serbia. It was quite difficult to get a ticket for one of those buses. You needed a good connection to get a ticket in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever the explanations may be, that's for Mr. Kehoe to ask further questions to you about that. So therefore please proceed. Mr. Waespi, if you want to refer to the second statement, if that's what was on your mind about the extra buses, where it specifically reads Belgrade, yes. That raises an another issue, Mr. Kehoe. To what extent it's necessary, but of course I leave it to you to what extent it's necessary to have the witness repeat what is already in evidence, that's in the 92 ter statement, or go direct to any further questions you would have on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The only issue, Judge, is that this is my only opportunity to address that which is in the 92 ter statements. And I'm certainly not going to go through all of those statements but just episodically cover several instances to get a bit more clarity on those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not in any way inviting you not to seek any further clarity but of course the first question is what the witness said to the OTP. She has testified before that the 92 ter statement reflects what she said. So therefore that question is -- unless there's any specific reason to doubt that it does reflect, answer the question to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you want me to refer to exactly where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not at all. To put -- apparently you have further questions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's immediately focus on those further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because what the witness told the Prosecution is -- we have read that in the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now in addition to these other people that were leaving in buses prior to Operation Storm, your relatives left on the 2nd of August, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was on the evening before Operation Storm. A relative of mine with three children below the age of 10 left, and one of the children was an infant still wearing nappies. I travelled to Serbia bringing back infant food while I had the opportunity to do so but at one point I stopped doing that. It was no longer possible because it was a long road to Belgrade. She had small children and it is quite natural that she tried to find a solution to improve their living conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, evacuation lists were not limited to just women and children, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're talking about the evacuation list of the UN members, because I know only about those evacuation lists of the United Nations staff members. I was on the list of the UN staff members. I was one of the few who had put my name on it. I didn't have any close family there, and I could leave Knin without any second thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, in fact you were on an evacuation list that was prepared by the special forces of the Republic of Serb Krajina as well, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I did mention that my boyfriend, at one point I was thinking about giving it all up, my boyfriend said that he could put me -- my name on the list, so if necessary I would be evacuated by somebody from his unit. But I don't know. I never checked whether he had actually put my name on the list, whether that list existed or not. I felt safe enough being on the United Nations' list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, your boyfriend was a member of the special forces, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He told you that he put you on an evacuation list two weeks prior to Operation Storm, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he would put my name on the list. I don't know whether he actually did that, because I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it is true, is it not, based on your knowledge that elements of the Republic of Serb Krajina were putting evacuation lists together at least two weeks prior to Operation Storm, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact. That may have referred to some privileged family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, that's in fact that being that evacuation lists had been prepared for two weeks. That's what your boyfriend told you on August the 4th of 1995 at about 1500 hours, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not what he told me at 3.00 on the 4th of August. At 3.00 on the 4th of August he begged me to leave the compound. The shells were falling all around us. We were not talking about evacuation lists. I don't know what means he was going to use for the two of us to escape, on foot, on a tractor. I don't know. I didn't check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your statement that was admitted into evidence, on page 2 of that statement, and I believe this is P2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's the 1996 statement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the 2007 statement, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, P3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you refer to the year, that will avoid whatever confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness, did you tell the Prosecution this information: "When I spoke to my boyfriend, which was about 3.00 p.m. on Friday afternoon, he told me that he and his friends were leaving the front line as it had been broken. About ten to 15 days earlier, he told me that he would place me on a special evacuation list. My understanding that the list included families of the Serbian Krajina Special Forces, which was the unit my boyfriend was in"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was a small unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you tell that to the Prosecutor when you took this statement on 11 June 2007?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I don't know whether the list actually existed, because I never saw my previous boyfriend again after that. I don't know if my name was on that list. I don't know how long the list was, but I know that the special unit was a very small one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But as far as you do know, there were elements of the Republic of Serb Krajina that were preparing evacuation lists to evacuate Knin, and family members of these units that lived in Knin. That's what he told you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relatives that I was living with were not on the evacuation list. My friends, my girlfriends, were not on the evacuation list, which doesn't mean that no one was on these evacuation lists. I'm just telling you what privileged family members were. If indeed the lists ever existed. This was a very small unit, as I said. Did he say this to hold me back? Did he say this to calm me down? Did the list exist or not? I don't know but it gave me some sort of a feeling of safety and made me stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move to a further subject on the 4th, and you said in response to some questions by my colleague, Mr. Waespi, that you made it to the UN compound, and I believe you told the Prosecutor in the first statement, P2, that the people began to come to the UN compound at 1800 hours on the night of the 4th. That would be 6.00 p.m. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. I do have to admit that my conscience did not allow me to go all the way to the gate and face those people standing just outside. I felt protected within the UN compound, and they were still out there standing outside the gate, exposed. But I do know that those were people with no fuel and people who were hoping in their naivety, just as I was, that nothing would befall them. They were seeking UN assistance and that's why they tried to position themselves right outside the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they began to -- they congregated there, according to your statement, at 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening hours but as I said I refused to go to the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now we talked about, and we will go back to the actual Operation Storm, and we talked about the evacuation. Let me just take you to a period of time staying on the subject of evacuation but later on in your statement. You noted in your statement that on August 16th, 16 August, 15 members of the Croatian parliament came to the UN to talk to displaced people to try to get them to remain in Croatia. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It would be helpful if my colleague had a reference for these exhibits. Do you have a paragraph, a page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is -- actually, it's one of the HRAT reports of 16 and the number 0060-4807.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are they exhibits at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then of course if you put it to the witness, the Chamber would appreciate if it could follow any quote from what apparently was a document so that we can check whether it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, this is in fact something that she was talking about in her statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you refer us to the portion of the statement where she talks about it? It's the 1996 or the 2007 statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just pulling the statement. I believe it's the 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Page number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am looking for it now, Judge. Your Honour, can my colleagues find this and I will come back to this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us -- let us move on a bit and we will come back to this particular point in a moment, but I would just like to move on a bit just to talk to -- about the interpreters as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted in your direct examination that you wanted to stay on because you were afraid that the UN would hire someone else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. My understanding was that if any of us left, we would no longer know what was going on. We weren't really conscious at the time what was going on throughout the Krajina. I didn't know if there was anyone left in the town itself, were we the only surviving group. I didn't know and I wanted to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you have some doubt that some other group of people could interpret exactly to the UN what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told specifically about the four of us, the four of us from the UN civilian police. We were told at a meeting that should we refuse to go on translating they would hire translators from Sibenik, which did, as a matter of fact, happen within a couple of days. There weren't enough of us to go around doing the interpretation, so some extra interpreters from Sibenik were hired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were concerned that Croats from Sibenik would be brought in to translate. Was that your concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats from Sibenik were in fact brought in. I remember the day they were. When I addressed them, I was told to explain their duties to them. I said, "One thing you should know is that you'll be coming across dead bodies." One of the interpreters then said, "That is impossible Operation Storm has now been concluded. There are no more dead people lying around." Several days later that same interpreter came back to me to confirm that he had indeed seen dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to an area and I'm not certain if it's going to be problematic concerning the witness's safety but I think in a spirit of caution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should guide the Chamber in this respect since we do not know where you go. So therefore out of an abundance of caution perhaps it's better to go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time with the assistance of the registry, I'd like to put an overhead of Knin on the ELMO. It was part of a larger presentation. And show it to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has it been uploaded into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has not, unfortunately. It will be because it is part of a series of exhibits that we are going to introduce into evidence. It is one shot of a montage of various -- of various aspects of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it might be easier if the witness looked at the ELMO because the picture is better than on her screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I agree. Your Honour, if I may, I could -- I am told by my courtroom deputy that we could give this to Your Honour in a clearer picture in colour, but we are going to have the particular witness write on this document. It's the same exact document. It has more clarity for the Court and the parties, and it may be a bit more helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Give us the best you have, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, and most important, is that the witness has a copy which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's a better copy, then it's primarily she who should be able to know exactly what she finds there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Madam Witness, you recognise that area from that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite clearly in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And from that photograph could you point to exactly where you were on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And could you take a pen and mark that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we are marking exhibits, we never know exactly if these are hard copies what colour is used. Red for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be fine, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would you give a red pen to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you do that for us, ma'am? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on that photograph, do you know where General Martic -- Mrksic's headquarters were for the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina? Do you know where it is from there? And if you can, can you mark it for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where his HQ was. There was one. I'm not sure if it was police or the army. It was on the main street, but I don't know who was based there. But it wasn't something that I wanted to know at the time. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, you were in fact an interpreter for the UN, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right but I did not go to any official meetings. I was a field interpreter and I would go out to the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you never learned during the course of your work where the headquarters were for the army of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm telling you is this: I know that on the main street there was some sort of an HQ. Was it police, was it army, I don't know. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where was that headquarters that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main street in Knin. Just further down the street from the department store there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Using the map that you have before you could you point that out and give that a number 2 for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might have been around here. This is the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, approximately how far was that place that you designated as number 2 from your house? How far is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UN office --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. How far was it from the first place where you made a point to where you put number 2? How far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A kilometre, perhaps. Up to a kilometre as the crow flies, but I really can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In between there, ma'am, there was a military supply depot, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know this as the Red Cross warehouse now. Whether this was the local or the International Red Cross, I don't know, because sometimes we would go there to pick up the humanitarian aid to take to the villages in Vrlika area. So that is the Red Cross warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. I mean, do you know, in fact, in that area if there was a supply depot for the army of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I think it was a Red Cross warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's just take a look at -- now, in fact, there was a parliament building in that area, too, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a building that had been reconstructed. I suppose it was the parliament building, but I was not really interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't know of your own personal knowledge if it was the parliament building or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not really interested in that. I was not in interested in the political or the military situation. I was helping the people in the field. I was a humanitarian worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, why don't you put down as number 3 the building that you know -- or you think is the parliament building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, there was also in that particular area a post office and telegraph building, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That was the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in and around your house there was a post office, a -- some type of military headquarters, and a parliament building in the general vicinity of your residence. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, but there was the kindergarten and the outpatient clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you're using the kindergarten. Let's talk about the kindergarten. The kindergarten building was in fact being used by the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't know that they in fact had troops and supplies in the building that was formerly used as a kindergarten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where is the kindergarten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was here. It was a park, and the kindergarten was somewhere around here. Should I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, ma'am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, it's marked with a 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk, ma'am, about the actual shelling on the 4th. You didn't see any of this shelling that took place on the morning of the 4th, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was quite sufficient for me to hear it. I was in my apartment, and I ran out into the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you didn't see it, did you, because you were in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the shelter, but at one point I went up to my apartment, which was on the third floor, with a Croatian lady, and I looked out of the window. I saw the shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when you ultimately had the opportunity to go through the Knin town, you told the Prosecutor in the first statement, and that would be, I believe, P2, Your Honour. That's the July 4 -- 4 July 1996. You noted to the Office of the Prosecutor that Knin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That Knin didn't seem to have suffered great damage. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, you're running and the shells are falling all around you. You don't have an opportunity to notice many things. I saw the destroyed house, the damage to the outpatient clinic, and I saw a house. There was a big hole in it. It was right there where I ran into a shelter. I can't recall any other details as I ran there and the shells were falling all around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
